title: A unique right factor from proportional oriented maximal minors

content.display_title: A unique right factor from proportional oriented maximal minors
content.one_sentence_role: Recovers a square factor and its determinant from proportional determinants of every ordered row tuple.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $A,B$ be $I$-by-$n$ matrices over a field and let $\lambda\ne0$. For an ordered tuple $\rho:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to I$, let $A_\rho,B_\rho$ be the selected square matrices, retaining the order and any repetitions in $\rho$. Assume

$$\det A_\rho=\lambda\det B_\rho\quad\text{for every }\rho.$$

Suppose one tuple $\rho_0$ satisfies $\det B_{\rho_0}\ne0$. There is a unique square matrix $L$ with $BL=A$ and $\det L=\lambda$.
content.assumptions: The coefficient system is any field; $I$ is any set, without an order or finiteness assumption. The scalar $\lambda$ is nonzero, proportionality holds for all ordered tuples, and the same chosen tuple $\rho_0$ supplies the nonzero minor. The case $n=0$ is included.
content.conclusion:
Writing $A_0=A_{\rho_0}$ and $B_0=B_{\rho_0}$, the factor is

$$L=B_0^{-1}A_0.$$

It satisfies $BL=A$ and $\det L=\lambda\ne0$, hence is invertible. The uniqueness already follows from $BL=A$.
content.proof_summary: Use the same nonzero selected minor to compare every row’s coordinates by Cramer’s rule. The coordinate equality supplies the global factorization; the selected square equation supplies its determinant and uniqueness.

proof_steps.text: Proportionality at $\rho_0$ gives $\det A_0=\lambda\det B_0$. Since $\lambda$ and $\det B_0$ are nonzero in a field, $\det A_0\ne0$. Thus both $A_0$ and $B_0$ are invertible. Define $L=B_0^{-1}A_0$; immediately $B_0L=A_0$.

Fix any row index $i\in I$ and write $a_i,b_i$ for the corresponding rows. For every position $j$, replace the $j$th entry of $\rho_0$ by $i$. The hypothesis applies even if this creates a repeated entry. The selected matrices are $A_0[j\leftarrow a_i]$ and $B_0[j\leftarrow b_i]$, so Cramer’s row formula gives

$$\begin{aligned}
(\det A_0)(a_iA_0^{-1})_j&=\det(A_0[j\leftarrow a_i])\\
&=\lambda\det(B_0[j\leftarrow b_i])\\
&=\lambda(\det B_0)(b_iB_0^{-1})_j
=(\det A_0)(b_iB_0^{-1})_j.
\end{aligned}$$

Cancellation of $\det A_0\ne0$ proves $a_iA_0^{-1}=b_iB_0^{-1}$.

Multiply the last row identity on the right by $A_0$:

$$a_i=(a_iA_0^{-1})A_0=(b_iB_0^{-1})A_0=b_iL.$$

It holds for every $i$, hence $BL=A$. Taking determinants in the selected equation $B_0L=A_0$ gives $(\det B_0)\det L=\det A_0=\lambda\det B_0$; canceling the nonzero factor $\det B_0$ yields $\det L=\lambda$.

If another matrix $L'$ satisfies $BL'=A$, selecting the same rows gives $B_0L'=A_0$. Multiplication by $B_0^{-1}$ forces $L'=B_0^{-1}A_0=L$. This proves uniqueness even before imposing the determinant condition.

To pass from increasing minors to arbitrary tuples when an order on $I$ is available, write an injective tuple as an increasing enumeration composed with a permutation $\sigma$. Both determinants gain the factor $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$, so their proportionality is unchanged. A noninjective tuple has two equal rows and both determinants vanish. For $n=0$, there is one empty tuple, both determinants are $1$, and the hypothesis reads $1=\lambda\cdot1$, forcing $\lambda=1$; the unique empty matrix is the required factor.

content.lean_realization_notes: If $I$ has a linear order, proportionality of the increasing-row minor families implies the ordered-tuple hypothesis: sorting an injective tuple introduces the same permutation sign for both matrices, while a repeated row makes both determinants zero. This adapter is separate from the theorem’s order-free assumptions. A nonzero selected minor also implies that multiplication by $B$ on column vectors is injective: restrict $Bv=0$ to the selected rows and multiply by $B_0^{-1}$.
